newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Tennis-struck OLOs face serving of new EMU concern.
newsitem.headline: Tennis-struck OLOs face serving of new EMU concern.

text.p: Belgian heroics in the French Open semifinals provided the excitement in Friday's government bond (OLO) and futures market where May's U.S. jobs report failed to set off as much as a single spark, dealers said.

Tennis player Filip Dewulf bravely defended his country's colours, still losing to Brazil's Gustavo Kuerten, while OLO traders were hardly called upon to lift a finger to cash in on long positions or close shorts after the jobs numbers.
However, hopes for a revival of business centre on Sunday's rare gathering in Luxembourg of EU finance ministers, under intense pressure to put the euro back on a solid footing.
The tennis game, which started at 1100 GMT, appeared to delay the market's reaction to the release of the jobs report at 1230 GMT, when the match was still on.
"Everybody was watching it...for many the figures were an annoying disturbance...nobody wanted to risk being skinned on (the benchmark) OLO 26 while the match was on," a trader said.

After the U.S. numbers -- a mixed bag with May much below forecasts, but April the subject of a large upward revision US-ECI -- no change in OLO futures prices BGB: was seen for 14 minutes. The market then joined a kneejerk sell-off. But the frontmonth was up 0.01 at 121.29 again at 1440 GMT.

The EMU concerns centre on the willingness of political heavyweights Germany and France to maintain their commitment to the euro currency's 1999 launch date and/or the tough Maastricht EMU entry criteria.

The position of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has been weakened by a row with the Bundesbank over a revaluation of gold assets, while there is uncertainty over the commitment of France's new left-wing government to the EU's stability pact.
"France and Germany will both not qualify (for EMU), which will mean Italy and Spain will be let in (if EU leaders still allow France and Germany to join)," a sceptical trader said.
"It will be a case of the lame leading the blind," he added.
Still, the political pressures to make the EMU project a success meant there was a distinct risk to selling off OLOs on worries about a possible delay, leaving the market in limbo.

"5.85 percent can be the bottom for the benchmark OLO, while at 6.00 percent buyers are waiting, even retail," the trader said. Given the stock markets' continuing bull run, bond volumes would remain thin, though.
One trader said the market was looking for price gains as an excuse to take profits. "In the last few days we have only seen buyers... professionals...a lot of longs have been set up."

He also said that once the 10-year OLO yield BE286= reached 5.85 percent positions would be sold. "Six percent then is not that far away." The 10-year benchmark yielded 5.89 percent at 1500 GMT, little changed from Thursday.

The Luxembourg EU meeting would be scrutinised. "It could cast a shadow over the market...there are some serious euro-sceptics in the French government now...but it would cause only a temporary back-up in yields," the trader said.
